suggestions.title: Excitotoxicity is calcium overload, not cells "vibrating to death"

edits.before: The Mechanism: Excess Glutamate over-activates NMDA receptors, acting like a key stuck in the "On" position. This causes "excitotoxicity"--literally vibrating cells to death. Subjectively, this feels like anxiety, rage, or an "itchy brain."
edits.after: The Mechanism: Excess Glutamate over-activates NMDA receptors, the doors on brain cells that glutamate unlocks, acting like a key stuck in the "On" position, so too much calcium pours into the cells. In extreme cases, like a stroke or a brain injury, that calcium overload kills them, which is what "excitotoxicity" means (Sattler & Tymianski, 2001). The anxiety, rage or "itchy brain" you feel in a glutamate storm is more likely the over-excitement itself than a sign your neurons are dying.

suggestions.what: Cells die because over-activated NMDA receptors let too much calcium in, and that happens in extreme cases like a stroke or a brain injury. The feelings stay, said as the over-excitement itself rather than neurons dying. NMDA receptors get a few words of explanation where they first come up in the section.
suggestions.why: Nothing vibrates: the cell is killed by the calcium the receptor lets in, and it matters in strokes, brain injury and neurodegeneration ([Sattler & Tymianski 2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1385/MN:24:1-3:107)). Nothing I found ties anxiety or rage to cells dying, and saying it does tells a reader their anxiety is brain damage.
suggestions.stays: The key stuck in the "On" position, the word excitotoxicity, and the anxiety, rage and "itchy brain".
suggestions.deciding: Whether the paragraph says what the cell death really is, and keeps the feelings as over-excitement.
suggestions.advice_note: Approve. It also sets up the calcium for the Lock below.

suggestions.title: GluD: a new finding, still argued over, and the armor part said as a guess

edits.before: The Signal Dial (GluD Receptors): Beyond the "voltage spike" of NMDA, Johns Hopkins researchers have recently discovered the brain uses GluD receptors as a master volume knob. While NMDA is the spark, GluD manages the baseline "hum" of the synapse. In an armored state, this dial is often jammed in the "High" position (Cerebellar Ataxia/Hyper-vigilance) or "Low" (Apathy/Schizotypy).
edits.after: The Signal Dial (GluD Receptors): So if NMDA is the spark, is anything else turning the signal up or down? Well according to a recent finding by Johns Hopkins researchers, GluD receptors, mainly known for helping build synapses, are also channels themselves, gates that let current into the cell, and what opens them is D-serine (one of the tools below) and GABA, the brain's main calming chemical, rather than glutamate (Wang, et al, 2025). Other researchers' tests the year before found no sign of that, so it's still being argued over (Itoh, et al, 2024). A mutation that causes cerebellar ataxia, a movement and balance disorder, leaves the channel leaking when it should be shut, and in schizophrenia GluDs seem to be less active than normal (Johns Hopkins, 2025). Whether an armored state jams it too, on "High" as hyper-vigilance or on "Low" as apathy and schizotypy (odd, schizophrenia-like thinking), nobody has tested, so that part is a hypothesis.

suggestions.what: This starts from your version, the one that read Human ([your check](https://www.pangram.com/history/f2a4727d-a109-46d4-a907-40efa6350e96)): your "Well according to", the label and the High/Low ending stay. What changes is what the finding says (GluDs are channels, opened by D-serine and GABA, not a volume knob), that it is still disputed, the two known cases, and that the armor part is a guess nobody has tested. Your version had dropped the link to the news story; I put a citation back, to the paper itself, since the paragraph rests on it.
suggestions.why: The paper ([Wang et al. 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12520249/)) found purified human GluD2 is a channel that D-serine and GABA open. A year earlier two labs tested the same idea and found no sign of direct gating ([Itoh et al. 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11295041)), so it is new and contested. The known cases: an ataxia mutation makes the channel leak, and in schizophrenia GluDs are less active ([Johns Hopkins](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/news/newsroom/news-releases/2025/09/scientists-find-potential-new-drug-target-for-psychiatric-and-neurological-disorders)). So your speculation makes sense on the Low side (schizotypy, less active); on the High side the only known case is a movement disorder, so hyper-vigilance there is a guess with nothing under it yet. It also gives the section a better reason to mention GluD: D-serine, one of your tools, opens it.
suggestions.stays: Your opening question's place, your "Well according to", the label, and the High/Low with its four states.
suggestions.deciding: Whether the paragraph says the finding as it is, with its dispute, and calls the armor part a hypothesis.
suggestions.advice_note: Approve. After that I humanize it from here, keeping your moves; it is longer than your version because the dispute and the two cases take room.

suggestions.title: D-cycloserine is a different drug from D-serine, and its boost is small

edits.before: D-serine may support therapeutic memory updating through NMDA-dependent learning mechanisms, while also engaging GluD receptors that regulate synaptic activity/tone. The specific drug form studied is D-cycloserine. which has evidence as an exposure-therapy augmenter because it can facilitate NMDA-dependent consolidation of extinction learning. It does not erase fear directly; it appears to strengthen whatever learning occurs during or after the exposure session. This is why session quality matters: if the exposure produces corrective learning and ends with reduced fear or mastery, DCS (and possibly D-serine also) may help consolidate that new memory; if the exposure is overwhelming or ends badly, it may consolidate the wrong association.
edits.after: D-serine may help therapy update old memories, because it switches on a spot on the NMDA receptor that this kind of learning needs (Wolosker, et al, 1999), and it may also open the GluD channels. The drug that's actually been tested with exposure therapy (facing the feared thing in small, safe doses) is a different one, D-cycloserine (DCS), which works on that same spot, and across 21 trials with over 1,000 patients it gave exposure therapy a small boost (Mataix-Cols, et al, 2017). It does not erase fear directly; it appears to strengthen whatever learning occurs during or after the exposure session. This is why session quality matters: if the exposure produces corrective learning and ends with reduced fear or mastery, DCS (and possibly D-serine also) may help consolidate that new memory; if the exposure is overwhelming or ends badly, it may consolidate the wrong association (Smits, et al, 2013).

suggestions.what: The drug tested with exposure therapy is named as a different one that works on the same NMDA spot as D-serine, not "the drug form" of it, and its effect is given as it was found: a small boost across 21 trials. Exposure therapy gets a few words of explanation. The session-quality rule stays word for word, now with its source.
suggestions.why: D-cycloserine (DCS) is its own drug that acts at the NMDA receptor's glycine spot, the spot D-serine switches on ([Smits et al. 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3747985); [Wolosker et al. 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC23961)). The best evidence, 21 trials with 1,047 patients, found a small boost ([Mataix-Cols et al. 2017](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/2599177)), and it helped after sessions that ended with low fear, not after the others, which is your session rule. I found no trial of D-serine itself with exposure therapy, which your "possibly" already covers.
suggestions.stays: "It does not erase fear directly" and the whole session-quality sentence, word for word.
suggestions.deciding: Whether DCS is named as a separate drug and its effect given as small.

suggestions.title: NAC works as a brake on glutamate release, not a vacuum

edits.before: The Fix ("Lock, Stock, and Barrel"):The Vacuum (NAC): Clears the flood by exchanging glutamate for cystine.
edits.after: The Fix ("Lock, Stock, and Barrel"):The Vacuum (NAC): It works less like a vacuum than a brake. NAC gives the brain's support cells cystine (an amino acid), which they swap for glutamate, and in rat studies that glutamate outside the synapse trips a brake (the mGluR2/3 receptors) that cuts how much glutamate gets fired into the synapse (Moran, et al, 2005).
NAC: 1.8g – 2.4g (divided doses). Turns down glutamate release.

suggestions.what: The Vacuum keeps its label, and the line says it works less like a vacuum than a brake, and how. The NAC dose line in the Glutamate Shield (block 119) changes its note from "Mops up glutamate" to "Turns down glutamate release"; the dose stays exactly as it is.
suggestions.why: The swap NAC drives puts more glutamate outside the synapse, not less; that glutamate trips a brake (mGluR2/3) that cuts how much glutamate is released into the synapse, in rats ([Moran et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1413952)). One rat study found the opposite at high concentrations, through another receptor (mGluR5), which is worth knowing but not a reason to change your dose ([Kupchik et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3340445)).
suggestions.stays: The "Lock, Stock, and Barrel" heading, the Vacuum label, and the dose, 1.8g – 2.4g (divided doses).
suggestions.deciding: Whether NAC is described as the brake it is.

suggestions.title: Magnesium plugs the channel; zinc mostly makes it open less

edits.before: The Lock (Zinc/Magnesium): Physically blocks the receptor channel to stop the voltage.
edits.after: The Lock (Zinc/Magnesium): Magnesium physically plugs the NMDA receptor's channel while the cell is at rest (Jalali-Yazdi, et al, 2018), and zinc mostly makes the channel open less often, with a weaker plug of its own (Amico-Ruvio, et al, 2011), so less of the voltage gets through.

suggestions.what: Says what each of the two does instead of both "physically blocking".
suggestions.why: Magnesium sits in the channel and plugs it until the cell is excited enough to push it out ([Jalali-Yazdi et al. 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6333211)). Zinc mainly binds outside and makes the channel open less often; its own plug is weaker ([Amico-Ruvio et al. 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21504727/)). Whether swallowing them changes this in the brain is a separate question the article doesn't claim, so I left it.
suggestions.deciding: Whether the two are told apart.

suggestions.title: L-serine stays with a corrected reason; leucine goes

edits.before: The Repair (Leucine/L-Serine): L-Serine is what the brain makes D-Serine from, so it can help recalibrate the GluD "Volume Dial" and make therapy sessions that end with low fear and a sense of mastery stick better. The conversion isn't very efficient though, so some people take D-serine itself instead (more risk, but also more benefit). And we use Leucine for structural repair, since it also tunes synaptic gain, which eases the "itchy brain" feeling.
edits.after: The Repair (L-Serine): L-Serine is what the brain makes D-Serine from (Wolosker, et al, 1999), so it can feed the spot on the NMDA receptor (and maybe the GluD channels) that D-serine switches on, and help therapy sessions that end with low fear and a sense of mastery stick better. The conversion isn't very efficient though, so some people take D-serine itself instead (more risk, but also more benefit).

suggestions.what: L-serine stays, now feeding the NMDA spot (and maybe the GluD channels) that D-serine switches on, instead of "recalibrating the GluD Volume Dial". Leucine comes out of the Repair and its label, with its reason. Leucine appears nowhere else in the article, so nothing else changes.
suggestions.why: The brain does make D-serine from L-serine ([Wolosker et al. 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC23961)), and the conversion really is weak (oral L-serine raised brain D-serine only a little in rats). But there is no volume dial (SB-38). For leucine I found nothing on "tuning synaptic gain". What I found points the other way: in rats at least half of the nitrogen in brain glutamate came from leucine ([2004 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14720211/)), and leucine competes with tryptophan and tyrosine, the raw materials for serotonin and dopamine, to get into the brain ([National Academies](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK209312/)). So for a protocol trying to calm glutamate, it isn't a repair.
suggestions.stays: L-serine, "sessions that end with low fear and a sense of mastery stick better", and the D-serine sentence with "more risk, but also more benefit".
suggestions.deciding: Whether leucine stays in the protocol. That one is yours: if you have a reason for it I didn't find, Revise and say it, and I will check it.
suggestions.advice_note: Approve, which cuts leucine. This paragraph read Human High as it stands, so after your answer it needs a humanizing pass and a new check.

suggestions.title: D-serine turns things up, not down

edits.before: Use D-Serine for acute sessions where you need to "force" memory reconsolidation. Best price from LifeLab. You should take it 45 minutes or so after taking PQQ & Ketones so that your brain is fueled when the GluD dial is turned down.
edits.after: Use D-Serine for acute sessions where you need to "force" memory reconsolidation. Best price from LifeLab. You should take it 45 minutes or so after taking PQQ & Ketones so that your brain is fueled when the D-serine starts working.

suggestions.what: The reason for the timing changes from "when the GluD dial is turned down" to "when the D-serine starts working". The timing itself, 45 minutes or so after PQQ & Ketones, stays exactly.
suggestions.why: D-serine opens the GluD channels and switches on the NMDA spot, so it turns them up ([Wang et al. 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12520249/); [Wolosker et al. 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC23961)); "turned down" said the opposite. One thing I left for later in Part 2: "force memory reconsolidation" is stronger than what the DCS trials show, which is help with consolidating new learning.
suggestions.stays: The scenario, the LifeLab link, and the timing.
suggestions.deciding: Whether the reason for the timing says the right direction.
